# Education in Poland
Education in Poland is structured around an extensive system of compulsory and secondary schooling. Primary school ("szkoła podstawowa") typically begins at age six or seven, following at least a year of kindergarten, and lasts eight years (grades 1–8). Previously, Poland employed a system of six years of primary school followed by three years of junior high school ("gimnazjum"), but a 2016 reform extended primary school to eight years and abolished gimnazjum. After completing primary education, students move to upper secondary education, which includes general secondary schools ("liceum") and vocational schools ("technikum" and "zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa"). General secondary programs last four years, culminating in the Matura exam that qualifies students for entry to higher education. Technical and vocational schools provide three to five years of education in specialized trades, and students can also pursue the Matura via supplementary study. Education is compulsory until the age of 18.
Tertiary education in Poland follows the Bologna structure: a three-year bachelor’s degree, a two-year master’s degree, and doctoral programs typically lasting three years, with some fields offering integrated long-cycle programs. University-level grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (pass with distinctions). Foreign language study is strongly emphasized in Polish schools—most students study English, German, French, or other languages. Notable historical milestones include the establishment of Jagiellonian University in 1364 and the introduction of the world’s first state ministry of education in 1773. Major reforms in 1999 and 2017 have shaped the current structure, with the most recent changes reversing earlier organizational shifts and adjusting curricula. The Polish state maintains a strong commitment to accessible education, with continued focus on literacy, compulsory schooling, and adaptation to European standards.
